subtopic: Integration as the inverse of differentiation, and the arbitrary constant
concept_tested: Reading the definition of an antiderivative in the correct direction
stem: Let $F$ be a function such that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[F(x)\right] = f(x)$ for every $x$ in an interval $I$. Then $\int f(x)\,dx$ on $I$ is

distractor_rationale.B: The student differentiates $F$ once more, confusing the antiderivative with the integrand.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates by differentiating, reversing the direction of the definition.
distractor_rationale.D: The student composes the two functions instead of recognising $F$ as the antiderivative of $f$.

solution: By definition $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on $I$, because differentiating $F$ returns $f$. Any two antiderivatives of $f$ on an interval differ by a constant, since a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant. Hence the complete family of antiderivatives is $F(x) + c$, and this family is what the symbol $\int f(x)\,dx$ denotes. The constant is added, not multiplied, because $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[F(x) + c\right] = f(x)$ while $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[c\,F(x)\right] = c\,f(x)$. Note also that $F'(x) + c$ is $f(x) + c$ and $f'(x) + c$ is the derivative of the integrand, neither of which is the required family.
formula_principle: Integration is the inverse process of differentiation. If $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[F(x)\right] = f(x)$, then $\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + c$, where $c$ is an arbitrary constant.
common_misconception: The student reverses the direction of the definition and differentiates the given function instead of naming its antiderivative.

subtopic: Integration as the inverse of differentiation, and the arbitrary constant
concept_tested: Two antiderivatives of the same function differ only by a constant
stem: To evaluate $\int \sec^{2}x\,\tan x\,dx$ one student puts $u = \tan x$ and gets $\dfrac{\tan^{2}x}{2} + c$, while another puts $u = \sec x$ and gets $\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2} + c$. Which of the following is true?

options.A: Only $\dfrac{\tan^{2}x}{2} + c$ is correct, because $u = \tan x$ is the only permissible substitution here.
options.B: Only $\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2} + c$ is correct, because $\sec^{2}x$ is the factor already present in the integrand.
options.C: Neither result is correct, because the two expressions are different functions.
options.D: Both results are correct, because the two expressions differ by a constant.

correct_answer_text: Both results are correct, because the two expressions differ by a constant.

distractor_rationale.A: The student believes an integral has exactly one algebraic form and rejects the second substitution.
distractor_rationale.B: The student picks the answer whose substitution looks closest to the integrand and rejects the other.
distractor_rationale.C: The student compares the two answers term by term and concludes that at least one must be wrong.

solution: With $u = \tan x$ we get $du = \sec^{2}x\,dx$, so the integral is $\int u\,du = \dfrac{u^{2}}{2} + c = \dfrac{\tan^{2}x}{2} + c$. With $u = \sec x$ we get $du = \sec x\tan x\,dx$ and the integrand is $\sec x\left(\sec x\tan x\right)dx = u\,du$, giving $\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2} + c$. Now $\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{2} - \dfrac{\tan^{2}x}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$, a constant. The two answers therefore describe the same family of antiderivatives, and differentiating either one returns $\sec^{2}x\tan x$.
formula_principle: If $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ are antiderivatives of the same function on an interval, then $F_{1}(x) - F_{2}(x)$ is a constant, so both are correct answers.
common_misconception: The student treats two antiderivatives that differ by a constant as contradictory answers, forgetting that the arbitrary constant absorbs the difference.

stem: A function $F$ satisfies $F'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ for $x > 0$ and $F(1) = 3$. Then $F(x)$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student uses the given value as a multiplier instead of as an added constant.
distractor_rationale.B: The student differentiates $\dfrac{1}{x}$ instead of integrating it, then fits the constant.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates $x$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{x}$, then fits the constant.

solution: Since $F'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$, we have $F(x) = \int \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \log|x| + c$. Putting $x = 1$ gives $F(1) = \log 1 + c = c$, and we are told $F(1) = 3$, so $c = 3$. common_misconception: The student multiplies the antiderivative by the given value instead of adding the constant that the initial condition forces.

concept_tested: The n = -1 case of the power rule

concept_tested: Identifying the single index for which the power rule breaks down
stem: The formula $\int x^{n}\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c$ is valid for every rational $n$ except one value. That value of $n$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student thinks $x^{0}$ cannot be integrated because the integrand is a constant.
distractor_rationale.B: The student guesses the smallest positive index.
distractor_rationale.C: The student thinks every negative index is excluded and names the first one after $-1$.

solution: The right hand side of the formula has $n + 1$ in the denominator, so it is meaningless precisely when $n + 1 = 0$, that is when $n = -1$. For $n = 0$ the formula gives $\int 1\,dx = x + c$, which is correct. For $n = 1$ it gives $\dfrac{x^{2}}{2} + c$, again correct. For $n = -2$ it gives $\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} + c = -\dfrac{1}{x} + c$, which is correct as well. Only $n = -1$ has to be replaced by the logarithmic result.
formula_principle: The power rule fails exactly when $n + 1 = 0$, and that case is covered by $\int x^{-1}\,dx = \log|x| + c$.
common_misconception: The student believes the power rule fails for all negative indices rather than for the single index $-1$.

concept_tested: Recognising an equivalent algebraic form of a standard trigonometric integral
stem: It is known that $\int \cot x\,dx = \log|\sin x| + c$. Which of the following is also a correct value of this integral?

distractor_rationale.A: The student converts $\sin x$ to $\csc x$ but keeps the sign unchanged.
distractor_rationale.C: The student interchanges the results for $	an x$ and $\cot x$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student replaces $\sin x$ by $	an x$, treating the two as interchangeable inside the logarithm.

solution: Since $\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$, we get $\log|\csc x| = \log\dfrac{1}{|\sin x|} = -\log|\sin x|$, hence $-\log|\csc x| = \log|\sin x|$. formula_principle: $\log|\sin x| = \log\left|\dfrac{1}{\csc x}\right| = -\log|\csc x|$, so the two forms of $\int \cot x\,dx$ agree.
common_misconception: The student rewrites $\sin x$ as $\csc x$ inside a logarithm without changing the sign in front.

subtopic: Integrals of the form 1/(x^2 - a^2) and 1/(a^2 - x^2)
concept_tested: Distinguishing the a^2 - x^2 form from the x^2 - a^2 form

distractor_rationale.A: The student applies the $x^{2}-a^{2}$ result to a denominator of the form $a^{2}-x^{2}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student uses $\frac{1}{a}$ in place of $\frac{1}{2a}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student treats the integrand as $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.

solution: With $a = 4$, $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{4^{2}-x^{2}} = \frac{1}{8}\log\left|\frac{4+x}{4-x}\right| + c$. Checking, $\frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{1}{4+x}+\frac{1}{4-x}\right) = \frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{8}{(4+x)(4-x)} = \frac{1}{16-x^{2}}$. Note that the two standard results differ in sign, so the order of the factors matters.
common_misconception: The student reads any difference of two squares in a denominator as the $x^{2}-a^{2}$ form and loses a sign.

subtopic: Integrals of the form 1/(x^2 - a^2) and 1/(a^2 - x^2)
concept_tested: Splitting a quartic denominator into the two standard quadratic forms

distractor_rationale.B: The student splits the fraction with a plus sign instead of a minus sign.
distractor_rationale.C: The student interchanges the two constants that come out of the split.

solution: Since $x^{4}-16 = (x^{2}-4)(x^{2}+4)$ and $(x^{2}+4)-(x^{2}-4) = 8$, we may write $\frac{1}{x^{4}-16} = \frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{1}{x^{2}-4}-\frac{1}{x^{2}+4}\right)$. Hence the integral is $\frac{1}{8}\left[\frac{1}{4}\log\left|\frac{x-2}{x+2}\right| - \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right] + c = \frac{1}{32}\log\left|\frac{x-2}{x+2}\right| - \frac{1}{16}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) + c$.
formula_principle: $\dfrac{1}{x^{4}-16} = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}-4}-\dfrac{1}{x^{2}+4}\right)$, then use the two standard results.
common_misconception: The student splits the algebraic fraction with the wrong sign, since the larger factor must be subtracted from the smaller one in the numerator.

subtopic: Integrals of the form 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2)
concept_tested: Two antiderivatives of 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2) that differ only by a constant
stem: For $|x| < 2$ a student evaluates $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}}$ and writes the answer as $-\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) + c$, while the textbook answer is $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) + c$. The student's answer is

options.B: incorrect, because $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ have different ranges and so different derivatives
options.C: correct only at $x = 0$, where the two expressions take the same value
options.D: correct, because the two expressions differ by the constant $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

correct_answer_text: correct, because the two expressions differ by the constant $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

distractor_rationale.A: The student forgets that the minus sign in the derivative of $\cos^{-1}$ cancels the minus sign written in front.
distractor_rationale.B: The student thinks a difference of ranges must mean a difference of derivatives.
distractor_rationale.C: The student checks a single point instead of comparing derivatives.

solution: Differentiate the student's answer: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[-\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right] = -\left(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{x^{2}}{4}}}\right)\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}}$, which is the integrand. So it is an antiderivative. Indeed $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}$, so $-\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) - \frac{\pi}{2}$. The two answers differ by a constant, which is absorbed in $c$, so both are correct.
common_misconception: The student believes that two antiderivatives written with different inverse functions must be different answers.

subtopic: Integrals of the form 1/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) and 1/sqrt(x^2 - a^2)
concept_tested: Two logarithmic forms of the same antiderivative of 1/sqrt(x^2 + 1)
stem: For $x > 0$ let $F(x) = \log\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right)$ and $G(x) = -\log\left(\sqrt{x^{2}+1}-x\right)$. Which one of the following is true?

options.B: $F(x)$ and $G(x)$ differ by a nonzero constant

distractor_rationale.B: The student assumes that any two antiderivatives on the same interval must differ by a nonzero constant.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads the minus sign in front of $G$ as reversing the derivative.
distractor_rationale.D: The student treats $G$ as the negative of $F$ because of the leading minus sign.

solution: Multiply and divide: $\sqrt{x^{2}+1}-x = \frac{\left(\sqrt{x^{2}+1}-x\right)\left(\sqrt{x^{2}+1}+x\right)}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}+x} = \frac{1}{x+\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}$. Taking logarithms, $\log\left(\sqrt{x^{2}+1}-x\right) = -\log\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right)$, so $G(x) = \log\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right) = F(x)$. The two expressions are identical, not merely equal up to a constant, so both are the same antiderivative of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}$.
common_misconception: The student stops at the leading minus sign and concludes that $G$ must be the negative of $F$.

stem: While resolving $\dfrac{3x+1}{(x-2)(x^{2}+4)}$ into partial fractions, the numerator taken over the factor $x^{2}+4$ must be

distractor_rationale.B: The student inserts a factor $\dfrac{1}{a}$ that belongs to the inverse tangent form, not to this one.
distractor_rationale.C: The student multiplies by $a$ instead of dividing by $a$ inside the inverse sine.
distractor_rationale.D: The student confuses $\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$ in the denominator with $a^{2}+x^{2}$.

solution: Put $x = 3\sin\theta$ with $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so $dx = 3\cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{9-x^{2}} = 3\cos\theta$, which is non negative on this range. The integral becomes $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3\cos\theta\,d\theta}{3\cos\theta} = \int d\theta = \theta + c = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3} + c$.
common_misconception: The student attaches the factor $\dfrac{1}{a}$ of the inverse tangent formula to the inverse sine formula.

subtopic: Trigonometric substitution, x = a sin theta, x = a tan theta, x = a sec theta
concept_tested: The secant substitution when the root is $\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}$

distractor_rationale.A: The student divides by $a$ instead of by $a^{2}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student inverts the ratio while returning from $\theta$ to $x$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student mishandles the sign of $\displaystyle\int\cos\theta\,d\theta$.

solution: Put $x = 3\sec\theta$ with $\theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so that $x > 3$. Then $dx = 3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{x^{2}-9} = 3\tan\theta$, which is positive here. The integral becomes $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta}{9\sec^{2}\theta \cdot 3\tan\theta} = \dfrac{1}{9}\int\cos\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{1}{9}\sin\theta + c$. Since $\sec\theta = \dfrac{x}{3}$, we get $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{x}$, so the answer is $\dfrac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{9x} + c$.
common_misconception: The student returns to $x$ using $\tan\theta$ rather than $\sin\theta$ and misplaces the root.

subtopic: Trigonometric substitution, x = a sin theta, x = a tan theta, x = a sec theta
concept_tested: The tangent substitution on a three halves power

distractor_rationale.A: The student divides by $a$ instead of by $a^{2}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates $\cos\theta$ as $-\sin\theta$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student inverts the ratio while converting $\sin\theta$ back to $x$.

solution: Put $x = 2\tan\theta$ with $\theta \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so $dx = 2\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta$ and $(x^{2}+4)^{3/2} = 8\sec^{3}\theta$. The integral becomes $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta}{8\sec^{3}\theta} = \dfrac{1}{4}\int\cos\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin\theta + c$. From $\tan\theta = \dfrac{x}{2}$ we get $\sin\theta = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}+4}}$, so the answer is $\dfrac{x}{4\sqrt{x^{2}+4}} + c$.
common_misconception: The student treats $(x^{2}+4)^{3/2}$ as $(x^{2}+4)\sqrt{x^{2}+4}$ but then applies the inverse tangent formula instead of the substitution.

subtopic: Mixed items combining substitution with a standard form
concept_tested: Exponential substitution leading to the inverse tangent standard form

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes the argument as $at$ instead of $\dfrac{t}{a}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student omits the factor $\dfrac{1}{a}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides by $a^{2} = 4$ instead of by $a = 2$.

solution: Put $t = e^{x}$, so $dt = e^{x}dx$ and $e^{2x} = t^{2}$. The integral becomes $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dt}{t^{2}+4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{2} + c = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{e^{x}}{2}\right) + c$.
formula_principle: Put $t = e^{x}$, so $e^{2x} = t^{2}$ and $dt = e^{x}dx$; then use $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dt}{t^{2}+a^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{a}$.
common_misconception: The student does not recognise $e^{2x}$ as the square of $e^{x}$ and so cannot see the standard form.

concept_tested: Exponential substitution followed by partial fractions

distractor_rationale.A: The two terms are written with interchanged signs.
distractor_rationale.B: The student integrates $-\dfrac{1}{t}$ in the new variable as $+\log|t|$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student changes the sign inside the logarithm while returning to $x$.

solution: Put $t = e^{x}$, so $dt = e^{x}dx$, that is $dx = \dfrac{dt}{t}$. The integral becomes $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dt}{t(t-1)}$. Resolving, $\dfrac{1}{t(t-1)} = \dfrac{1}{t-1} - \dfrac{1}{t}$, so the integral is $\log|t-1| - \log|t| + c = \log|e^{x}-1| - \log\left|e^{x}\right| + c = \log|e^{x}-1| - x + c$.
common_misconception: The student forgets that $dx = \dfrac{dt}{t}$ introduces an extra factor $\dfrac{1}{t}$ and so never gets the term $-x$.

subtopic: Mixed items combining substitution with a standard form
concept_tested: Multiplying by a suitable power to create a substitution

distractor_rationale.A: All the signs are reversed.
distractor_rationale.C: The student adds the two logarithms.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides both logarithms by $4$, forgetting that $\dfrac{1}{4}\log x^{4} = \log|x|$.

solution: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by $x^{3}$: the integral is $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x^{3}\,dx}{x^{4}(x^{4}+1)}$. Put $t = x^{4}$, so $dt = 4x^{3}dx$ and the integral becomes $\dfrac{1}{4}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dt}{t(t+1)} = \dfrac{1}{4}\int\left[\dfrac{1}{t} - \dfrac{1}{t+1}\right]dt = \dfrac{1}{4}\log|t| - \dfrac{1}{4}\log|t+1| + c$. Restoring $t = x^{4}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{4}\log\left|x^{4}\right| - \dfrac{1}{4}\log|x^{4}+1| + c = \log|x| - \dfrac{1}{4}\log|x^{4}+1| + c$.
formula_principle: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by $x^{3}$ and put $t = x^{4}$, so that $dt = 4x^{3}dx$.
common_misconception: The student attempts a direct partial fraction split in $x$ and cannot handle the factor $x^{4}+1$.

concept_tested: Choosing the substitution for a rational function of sin x of the first degree
stem: The integral $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{3+4\sin x}$ is best evaluated by using

distractor_rationale.A: This works only when $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ occur in even powers; here $\sin x$ occurs to the first power.
distractor_rationale.C: This substitution is meant for algebraic integrands containing $\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$.
distractor_rationale.D: There is no rational function of $x$ here, so the denominator cannot be factorised in $x$.

solution: Here $\sin x$ appears to the first power, an odd power, so the denominator is not a function of $\sin^{2}x$ and $\cos^{2}x$ alone. The half angle substitution $t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}$, with $\sin x = \dfrac{2t}{1+t^{2}}$ and $dx = \dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}$, converts the integral into a rational function of $t$ that can then be handled by partial fractions. The substitution $t = \tan x$ is reserved for denominators built from $\sin^{2}x$, $\cos^{2}x$ and $\sin x\cos x$.
formula_principle: A rational function of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ in which either occurs to an odd power is reduced by $t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}$.
common_misconception: The student uses $t = \tan x$ for every trigonometric denominator, without checking the parity of the powers involved.

concept_tested: Recognising an improper rational function
stem: To evaluate $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^{3}+2}{x^{2}-1}\,dx$, the first step must be to

options.A: divide $x^{3}+2$ by $x^{2}-1$ and then resolve the remainder term into partial fractions
options.B: resolve the integrand into partial fractions with denominators $x-1$ and $x+1$ at once
options.C: put $x^{2}-1 = t$, since the denominator is a function of $x^{2}$
options.D: put $x = \tan\theta$, to remove the quadratic denominator

correct_answer_text: divide $x^{3}+2$ by $x^{2}-1$ and then resolve the remainder term into partial fractions

distractor_rationale.B: The student applies partial fractions to an improper fraction, where no such decomposition exists.
distractor_rationale.C: The numerator is not a constant multiple of the derivative of the denominator, so this substitution fails.
distractor_rationale.D: A trigonometric substitution is meant for irrational integrands, not for a rational function like this one.

solution: The degree of the numerator, three, is greater than the degree of the denominator, two, so the integrand is an improper rational function. Division gives $\dfrac{x^{3}+2}{x^{2}-1} = x + \dfrac{x+2}{x^{2}-1}$, and only then is the remainder term proper and fit for a partial fraction decomposition into $\dfrac{P}{x-1} + \dfrac{Q}{x+1}$.
formula_principle: Partial fractions apply only to a proper fraction, so an improper rational function must be divided first.
common_misconception: The student begins the partial fraction work at once and finds an identity that cannot be satisfied for all $x$.

subtopic: Method selection across the whole chapter
concept_tested: Distinguishing a derivative substitution from a partial fraction problem
stem: The integral $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x+3}{x^{2}+3x+7}\,dx$ is best evaluated by

options.A: resolving the integrand into partial fractions with two distinct linear factors
options.B: putting $x^{2}+3x+7 = t$, since the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator
options.C: completing the square and then putting $x = a\tan\theta$
options.D: dividing the numerator by the denominator first

correct_answer_text: putting $x^{2}+3x+7 = t$, since the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator

distractor_rationale.A: The discriminant $9-28$ is negative, so the denominator has no real linear factors.
distractor_rationale.C: This is needed only when the numerator is a constant, not when it is the derivative of the denominator.
distractor_rationale.D: The fraction is already proper, since the numerator has the lower degree.

solution: The discriminant of $x^{2}+3x+7$ is $9 - 28 = -19 < 0$, so the denominator cannot be split into real linear factors and partial fractions of the usual kind are unavailable. Observe instead that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}+3x+7\right) = 2x+3$, exactly the numerator. Putting $t = x^{2}+3x+7$ gives $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|t| + c = \log\left|x^{2}+3x+7\right| + c$.
common_misconception: The student sees a quadratic denominator and starts a partial fraction decomposition without testing the discriminant.
